analysis.one_liner: Expands and renews government health insurance for low-income children, paid for by higher tobacco taxes.
analysis.headline: Both chambers passed the bill twice with bipartisan majorities, but President Bush vetoed it and the House's 273-156 override vote on October 18 fell short of the two-thirds needed.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill reauthorizes the Children's Health Insurance Program through 2012 at sharply higher funding, helps states enroll eligible but uninsured children, adds dental and mental health benefits, and lets states cover low-income pregnant women. It pays for this by raising federal excise taxes on cigarettes and other tobacco products. Both chambers passed it, the president vetoed it, and the House could not muster the two-thirds vote to override.
analysis.who_benefits: Low-income uninsured children and pregnant women, who gain health coverage through CHIP and Medicaid; states, which get larger federal allotments, enrollment bonuses, and new enrollment tools; military families, who gain caregiving leave and job protections; and community health centers, which get paid under a standardized prospective payment system [S6]. The bill's stated purpose is to enroll all six million uninsured children who are eligible but not enrolled [S7].
analysis.who_benefits_short: Low-income uninsured children and pregnant women

how_it_helps.text: Reauthorizes CHIP through fiscal year 2012 with annual allotments rising from $9.125 billion in 2008 to $13.75 billion in 2011, plus a one-time $12.5 billion appropriation for fiscal 2012 [S7].

Requires CHIP coverage to include dental services and establishes mental health parity in CHIP plans, and mandates a 30-day grace period before coverage can be terminated for nonpayment of premiums [S6].
Gives states options to cover targeted low-income pregnant women, simplify citizenship verification, and automatically enroll children born to mothers already receiving CHIP pregnancy coverage [S6].

Pays states performance bonuses for enrolling and retaining more children and creates a contingency fund for states that run short, while rewarding states that remove enrollment barriers like in-person interviews and asset tests [S7].
Provides family leave and job protection — up to 52 workweeks — for family members caring for injured servicemembers [S6].
Restricts CHIP-funded coverage of childless adults and caps the federal matching rate for states covering children above 300% of the poverty line, focusing the program on low-income children [S6].

analysis.who_pays: Smokers, who are disproportionately lower-income, pay higher federal excise taxes on cigarettes, cigars, smokeless and pipe tobacco, including a one-time floor-stocks tax on tobacco held by retailers [S6]. Tobacco manufacturers and importers face the higher rates plus new permit, recordkeeping, and payment rules [S6].

drawbacks.text: Tobacco taxes are regressive: lower-income smokers bear the cost of a children's health program, which critics note means one low-income group helps fund another's coverage [S6].

Expanding public coverage can substitute for private insurance — 'crowd-out' — and the bill itself devotes reporting requirements and best-practice standards to limit that substitution, acknowledging the tradeoff [S6].
The President vetoed the bill after it cleared both chambers, arguing the expansion went too far; his objections were the basis for the failed override [S9][S17].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core tradeoff is straightforward: millions of low-income children would gain coverage, paid for by taxes concentrated on smokers. The bill deliberately narrowed its reach — phasing out childless-adult coverage and capping matching rates for families above 300% of poverty — to address cost and crowd-out concerns. The main honest objection is the regressivity of tobacco taxes; the main cost of the bill's failure is that the expanded funding, enrollment bonuses, dental and mental health benefits, and enrollment simplifications never took effect.

outcome.mechanism: The House passed it 360-45 in February, the Senate rewrote it as a CHIP expansion and passed it 68-31, both chambers agreed to the final version in late September, but President Bush vetoed it and the House's October 18 override attempt got 273 votes when it needed about 290.

narrative.text: The House passed the original small-business tax bill 360-45 under suspension of the rules on February 16, 2007, with every Democrat voting yes and 141 of 201 Republicans in favor [S10].

The Senate replaced the bill's contents with the Children's Health Insurance Program Reauthorization Act and passed it 68-31 on August 2, with all 49 Democrats and 18 of 49 Republicans in favor [S5][S12].

The House agreed to the Senate amendments with amendments 265-159 on September 25, and the Senate accepted the House changes 67-29 on September 27, clearing the bill for the White House [S13][S15][S9].
President Bush vetoed the bill on October 3, 2007 [S9].
The House vote to override the veto failed on October 18: 273-156, short of the two-thirds required, with 229 of 233 Democrats in favor and only 44 of 200 Republicans [S17].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Tobacco companies kept lower excise taxes, and the House Republicans who sustained the veto kept CHIP from expanding; low-income children got none of the new funding, dental benefits, or enrollment help the bill would have provided.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Tobacco companies and veto-sustaining House Republicans

for.name: Charles Rangel
for.role: U.S. Representative (D-NY), Chair of Ways and Means, bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Sponsored the bill, steered it through the Ways and Means Committee to a 360-45 House passage in two days, and later managed the House agreement to the Senate amendments [S1][S9][S10].

for.name: 219 of 232 House Democrats
for.role: House Democratic caucus on final passage
for.what_they_did: Voted yes on passage, 219-0, on February 16, and 220 of 232 voted yes on the conference-level agreement in September [S10][S13].

for.name: 141 of 201 House Republicans
for.what_they_did: Voted yes on the February 16 passage vote [S10].

for.name: 48 of 49 Senate Democrats
for.what_they_did: Voted unanimously to pass the Senate version on August 2 and 47 of 49 voted yes on the final version on September 27 [S12][S15].

for.name: 18 of 49 Senate Republicans
for.what_they_did: Voted yes on the Senate version and on final passage; a further 19 Republicans joined all Democrats on the 80-0 cloture vote to proceed [S11][S12][S15].

against.name: George W. Bush
against.what_they_did: Vetoed the bill on October 3, 2007, after it cleared both chambers [S9].

against.name: 154 of 200 House Republicans
against.role: House Republicans on the override vote
against.what_they_did: Voted no on October 18 to override the veto, denying the two-thirds majority needed to enact the bill over it [S17].

against.name: 31 of 49 Senate Republicans
against.what_they_did: Voted no on the Senate version on August 2 and 29 of 49 voted no on the final version on September 27 [S12][S15].

sides.party_line_note: Democrats were near-unanimous at every stage; Republicans were split in February (141 of 201 for passage) but opposition hardened — only 18-19 Senate Republicans and 44-45 House Republicans supported the final bill and the override. Right after the veto, all 222 House Democrats voted to postpone the override debate while all Republicans present voted against it [S14 roll 938 → S16].

industries.note: The bill raises federal excise taxes on cigarettes, cigars, smokeless and pipe tobacco to fund children's coverage, and imposes new permit, recordkeeping, and payment rules on manufacturers and importers. Because the industry's cost is the program's funding source, its interest in the bill ran against the children who would have been covered [S6][S7].

industries.industry: Health insurers and managed care plans
industries.note: More CHIP enrollment means more customers for the private managed care plans that deliver most CHIP care, and state premium-assistance options subsidize employer-sponsored private coverage. The bill also applies Medicaid managed care quality safeguards to CHIP and requires special enrollment periods in employer plans, so private plans gain revenue while accepting new rules [S6].

industries.industry: Federally qualified health centers and rural health clinics
industries.note: The bill applies the Medicaid prospective payment system to CHIP, giving community clinics a standardized, generally higher payment rate for serving enrolled children [S6].
